title: The covered cistern
body:
We caught the same rain in two places. The barrel by the fields stood open; the cistern beneath the roof stayed shut. Only the barrel grew a green ring and left the dog unwilling to drink.

I promised to paint the cistern lid when the weather cleared. It seems absurd now that I was worried about the color.

title: The first bucket from the ditch
body:
Water from the low ditch left grit in our kitchen pail. The well water was clear. My father drank the ditch water at work and spent the next morning unable to stand.

I saved the grit in a little jar. He called it a waste of a good jar and asked me to bring him the well water instead.

title: The rain after spraying
body:
The sprayed field ran into the pond during the storm. The pond fish floated up the next morning, but the pond behind the hill still had them moving below the surface.

My nephew had planned to fish both ponds. I took away his net and told him we'd go when the water was clear.

title: The hose switch
body:
The gardener filled six watering cans from the field line and four from the house tap. Only the beds watered from the field line lost their new leaves.

The gardener says the cans were identical. I checked the roots because I wanted him to be wrong; he was already upset about the plants.

title: The cup in the greenhouse
body:
The greenhouse well was capped for repairs, so the workers used the open tank outside the trial rows. Three complained of a bitter taste before their afternoon break; the repair crew drank from a jug brought from home.

I brought the jug myself. It stayed half full, and I kept wishing I had brought enough for everyone.

title: The opposite bank
body:
A thin layer of pale dust settled on the downstream bank after the fields were washed. The upstream bank had only the usual silt. The chickens pecked at the lower bank and would not eat supper.

I had gone down there to collect smooth stones for my daughter. I left the stones and came back for the birds.

title: The uncovered rain dish
body:
I set out two dishes for the dog, one beneath the eaves and one beside the field gate. The gate dish gathered green specks overnight. The dog sniffed it and drank the covered one dry.

The gate dish was a wedding gift and I felt foolish testing rain in it. I washed it twice and the mark came back when it dried.

title: The clay in the kettle
body:
The family by the lower road asked me to boil their water. A green ring stuck inside the kettle. My own well water boiled in it before without leaving a mark.

Their youngest carried the kettle to my door because his mother was too weak. I put it on the stove before he had finished speaking.

title: The neighbor's fish
body:
The ditch by the seeded field held dead minnows in the shallows. The creek beyond the ridge still had live fish. My neighbor wanted to blame the heat, though both waters were under the same sun.

We had meant to take the children wading. I folded their towels away and kept the little sketch I made of the two channels.

title: The closed reservoir
body:
When the new field powder arrived, the water trough nearest the mixing shed developed a chalky edge. The closed reservoir at the far end did not. The animals pushed past one another to drink from the far one.

I was asked to check the fences, so I did. I also wrote down where each trough was filled; that part was my own idea.
